warmup.q: A program is writing 200 files of payments into dt=2026-11-07/, the folder that holds 7 November in a table kept as folders of files. Halfway through, a report reads that day. What does it see?
options: Nothing from that day, because the program locks the folder while it writes
Whatever files have landed so far: part of the program's payments
All 200 files, because the report waits for the program to finish
An error, because the folder is being written
warmup.why: When a folder is the table, the table is whatever files the folder holds right now, and files land one at a time as the program's workers finish. Nothing locks the folder and nothing waits, so a reader can see part of a write. That's the gap a table format closes. In Iceberg, readers see only the files that a committed version of the table lists, and a new version appears in one step. The lock is the tempting answer, because databases use locks, but a folder of files in cloud storage has nothing that could hold one.

sections.h: Why a folder makes a shaky table, and the list of files that fixes it
sections.html:
Warehouses and dimensional models ended on the one thing a warehouse does quietly: it keeps each table's list of files, and changes that list all at once. Many companies keep their analytics data somewhere cheaper, in a data lake: files in object storage. Object storage is a cloud service that keeps files (it calls them objects) cheaply and safely, such as S3, Amazon's. The files are usually Parquet, a common file format for tables stored by column. Nobody sits in front of them keeping a list.

So for years, a table in a lake was a folder. Hive: SQL on files, partitions and the metastore (lesson 4 of this track) met Hive. It was the first popular program for asking questions of files in SQL, the language most databases understand. (A question written in SQL is called a query.) Hive treats every file in a table's folder as part of the table. That lesson ended with three cracks in the idea. A write isn't atomic, meaning all-or-nothing. A job, one run of a program over the data, puts its files down one by one, and a reader in the middle sees part of the job. Listing is slow: on S3, one request returns at most 1,000 names, so a folder of 50,000 files takes 50 requests before the first byte of data. And columns are matched by name or by position, so renaming one means rewriting files or confusing readers. All three come from one decision: whatever is in the folder is the table.

Version 1: keep a list. Next to the data, write a file that names every data file of the table. Readers read the list instead of the folder, which fixes the slow listing. But a writer still has to change the list, and a reader can catch it half rewritten.

Version 2: never change a file; write a new one. This is the café's board in the back room. A write first puts down its new data files, which nobody reads, because no list names them. Then it writes a complete new list, which nobody reads yet either. Then it switches readers from the old list to the new one in a single step. Before the switch, every reader sees the old table; after it, the new one. Nobody can see half.

That single step needs one small thing that can change: a pointer that says which list is current. It also needs a safe way to change it, called compare-and-swap: set the pointer to a new value only if it still holds the value you read. Everything else is files written once and never edited. That's the design of a table format, a set of rules for keeping a table's file list, columns and history in files next to the data.

Apache Iceberg is a table format, and so are Delta Lake and Apache Hudi, two others built the same way that the next lesson compares. This lesson uses Iceberg, which almost every engine reads and writes. An engine is a program that runs questions over data. Two of them appear here: Spark, which spreads one big job over many computers, and DuckDB, a small analytics database that runs inside your own program.

The Try it shows the difference. A reader thread, a second line of work inside the same program, counts rows over and over while a writer adds 8 files. First the files are copied into a plain Parquet folder one at a time, the way a job's workers drop their output as they finish. The reader saw 3,000, 5,000, 6,000 and 7,000 rows on the way to 8,000. Those were tables that never existed. Appended to an Iceberg table in three commits of 8 files (a commit is one change made visible), the reader saw 0, 8,000, 16,000 and 24,000: whole commits, and nothing in between.

Iceberg itself is a specification, a document that says how the files are laid out, plus code libraries that follow it. It isn't a server or an engine: the table is files in your own storage. Whatever holds the pointer is called the catalog. It can be as simple as a folder, which is what this lesson uses. A Hadoop catalog keeps the whole warehouse as a tree of folders on your disk. It's named after Hadoop, the older big data system it was first written for. The demos and the lab use Iceberg 1.12.0 (September 2026) with Spark 4.1.4, the newest Spark that Iceberg 1.12 supports, as Spark 4 for JVM engineers explained.

A list of files works, but a big table has millions of files. Next, we'll see how Iceberg keeps its list from becoming one giant file.

try.title: Count rows while a writer adds files
steps: From the labs folder, run AtomicCommitDemo. A reader thread counts rows in a loop while the main thread adds files: first to a plain Parquet folder, one file a second, then to an Iceberg table, in three commits.
Predict the set of counts the reader will see in each case.
In the plain folder, each file appears whole: it's written under a hidden name, then renamed into place. Why does the reader still see part of a write?

code.title: AtomicCommitDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l11.demo import java.io.File import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentSkipListSet import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import kotlin.concurrent.thread /** * A reader counts rows in a loop while a writer adds 8 files. First into a plain Parquet folder, * one file a second, the way a job's tasks publish their files as they finish. Then into an * Iceberg table, as one commit. Prints every count the reader saw. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() val staged = File("build/l09/staged").apply { deleteRecursively() } payments(spark, 0, 8_000, files = 8).write().parquet(staged.absolutePath) // 8 files of 1,000 rows val files = staged.listFiles { f -> f.name.endsWith(".parquet") }!!.sorted() fun watch(count: () -> Long, write: () -> Unit): Set<Long> { val seen = ConcurrentSkipListSet<Long>() val done = AtomicBoolean(false) val reader = thread { while (!done.get()) runCatching { seen += count() } } Thread.sleep(500) write() Thread.sleep(500) done.set(true) reader.join() return seen } // a folder table: the file listing IS the table, so every new file is visible the moment it lands val folder = File("build/l09/plain").apply { deleteRecursively(); mkdirs() } val schema = spark.read().parquet(staged.absolutePath).schema() val plain = watch({ spark.read().schema(schema).parquet(folder.absolutePath).count() }) { for (f in files) { // copy under a hidden name, then rename: each single file appears whole val tmp = File(folder, ".${f.name}.tmp") f.copyTo(tmp) tmp.renameTo(File(folder, f.name)) Thread.sleep(1_000) // a task finishing every second } } println("plain folder, 8 files added one by one, the reader saw: $plain") // an Iceberg table: the files are written first, then one commit makes all of them visible spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.atomic ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg") val iceberg = watch({ spark.table("lake.pay.atomic").count() }) { repeat(3) { spark.read().parquet(staged.absolutePath).writeTo("lake.pay.atomic").append() } } println("Iceberg table, 3 commits of 8 files each, the reader saw: $iceberg") spark.stop() }

plain folder, 8 files added one by one, the reader saw: [0, 3000, 5000, 6000, 7000, 8000]
Iceberg table, 3 commits of 8 files each, the reader saw: [0, 8000, 16000, 24000]

In the plain folder, every file landed whole, and the reader still saw tables that never existed. When the folder is the table, each new file counts the moment it lands, and a job of 8 files is 8 separate moments. Which counts in between you catch depends on how fast your computer runs the reader's queries, so your list will differ. What matters is that it has values between 0 and 8,000. The Iceberg reader only ever saw multiples of 8,000. Each commit wrote its 8 files first, where no version of the table pointed at them, then made all of them visible in one swap.

aside.title: If a warehouse already does this, why build it out of files?
aside.html: Cost and openness. Files in object storage are cheap to keep, and any engine that knows the format can read them, so one table can serve Spark, DuckDB and a warehouse at the same time. In a warehouse, the data sits inside one company's product, and other tools reach it through that product. For years, many companies kept both, a lake of raw files and a warehouse loaded from it: two copies that drift apart. A table format gives the lake the warehouse's all-or-nothing changes, so one copy can do both jobs. A 2021 paper named that idea the lakehouse.

sections.h: Inside the list: a tree of files that are never edited
sections.html:
Version 2 had one list file. Keep the list as one file, and every commit must rewrite all of it: a table of a million files gets a new million-line list for a commit that adds ten. Iceberg splits the list into a tree, so a commit rewrites only a small top and reuses everything below it.

From the top, as the figure shows:

  1. The table metadata file, such as v4.metadata.json. Metadata is data about the data, and JSON is a text format of names and values. There's one metadata file per version of the table. It holds the schemas, the lists of columns, where each column has a permanent number of its own, its field id. It holds the partition specs, rules for grouping the data files by a value such as the day, which the last section opens up. It holds the table's settings, and the list of snapshots, the table's versions. Each snapshot has an id, its parent's id, a time, a summary and the location of its manifest list. One snapshot is the current one.
  2. The manifest list, one per snapshot, in Avro, a compact format that stores records one after another, with the column layout in the file's header. It has one row per manifest, with the range of partition values inside it, so a question about one day can skip whole manifests without opening them.
  3. The manifests, also in Avro, with one row per data file: its location, its partition value, its row count, its size, and statistics for each column, including the smallest and largest value. They're the min and max from Columnar files: Parquet internals and pushdown (lesson 5), moved up into the table's metadata, so a reader can skip a data file without opening it.
  4. The data files: plain Parquet.

A commit that appends 8 files writes 8 data files and one new manifest that lists them. It also writes one new manifest list, naming the new manifest plus all the old ones, and one new metadata file. The old manifests are reused as they are. That's why snapshots are cheap: two snapshots share every manifest that didn't change.

A reader walks the tree from the top. It reads the pointer, the metadata file, the current snapshot and its manifest list. Then it opens only the manifests whose partition ranges can match, and only the data files whose statistics can match. It never lists a folder. That cuts both ways. A file someone copies into the folder by hand is invisible to every reader, and a file someone deletes by hand breaks every snapshot that still lists it. The snapshot is the table, not the folder. Change the table through Iceberg.

In the Try it, creating a table and making three appends left four metadata files, one per version. It also left three manifest lists (one per snapshot), three manifests and nine data files, three days of payments per append. Spark also lets you query the tree as tables of their own: lake.pay.payments.snapshots, .manifests, .files and .history.

In café terms, a snapshot is a whole board, and the data files are the price cards pinned on it. The picture breaks in a useful place. A café throws its old board away, while Iceberg keeps old snapshots, and they share most of their cards with the new one. Next, we'll watch a commit build a new snapshot, and see what happens when two writers try at once.

sections.h: Committing a change: one swap of the pointer, even when two writers race
sections.html:
Everything in the tree is written once and never changed. The only thing a commit changes is the pointer, and that's where two writers meet.

Here's a commit, step by step, as the stepper shows. Write the data files. Write a manifest that lists them. Write a manifest list for the new snapshot. Write the new metadata file, which lists the new snapshot as current and keeps the old ones. Up to here, nobody can see anything new. Then swap the pointer from the old metadata file to the new one, if and only if it still names the old one. That condition makes the swap a compare-and-swap, and it's the whole commit protocol, the agreed set of steps.

What if two writers start from version 7 at once? Both build their new metadata on v7. The first to swap wins, and the table moves to v8. The second swap fails, because the pointer no longer says v7. The loser doesn't wait for a lock, a flag that makes everyone else wait their turn. It reloads v8, checks that its change still makes sense (for an append, it always does), applies it again on top of v8, and swaps again. This is optimistic concurrency: no locks while working, a check at the end, and a retry when the check fails. Iceberg's documentation calls the result serializable isolation: all changes line up in one order, as if they had happened one at a time. The retry is cheap, because the data files and the new manifest are reused, and only the small files at the top are written again.

Where the pointer lives depends on the catalog. In this lesson's Hadoop catalog, it's the metadata files themselves. A commit writes v8.metadata.json under a temporary name and renames it into place, and the rename fails if v8 already exists. Then version-hint.text tells readers where to start. That needs an all-or-nothing "create only if nobody has". HDFS, the file system Hadoop spreads over many machines, offers it through rename, and so does your laptop.

Object storage didn't. HDFS and MapReduce: the ideas that survived (lesson 3) showed that an object store isn't a file system. For years, S3 had no rename at all and no way to say "only if absent", so two writers could both write v8, and the last one silently won. That's why Delta Lake's documentation for S3 still asks that every writer of a table go through one Spark program, or through a lock table in DynamoDB, Amazon's database service.

Since 2024, S3 has conditional writes. A write with If-None-Match: * creates a file only if nothing has that name yet (August 2024). A write with If-Match replaces a file only if its ETag, a fingerprint S3 keeps for each version of a file, is still the one you read (November 2024). Those are exactly the two kinds of compare-and-swap a commit needs: "create v8 only if nobody has" and "move the pointer only if it still names v7". Real Iceberg tables still keep the pointer in a catalog backed by a database or a service. The catalog also names the tables, controls who may read them and serves every engine. Row-level changes, compaction and catalogs, the next lesson, covers those catalogs.

The old snapshots are still in the metadata, and each one still names exactly the files it had. That gives you time travel: SELECT ... FROM t VERSION AS OF <snapshot id>, or TIMESTAMP AS OF '<time>', reads the table as it was then. Readers also get isolation for free. A query that started on snapshot S1 keeps reading S1's files, even if S2 commits halfway through. The window closes when old snapshots are expired and their files deleted, a clean-up job the next lesson covers too.

Commits keep the table whole. Next, we'll see that the same metadata lets a table change its columns and its layout without rewriting a byte of data.

try.title: Lose a commit race, then read the past
steps: From the labs folder, run CommitDemo. Two writers load the same version of a table. Writer A changes a table setting with Iceberg's low-level commit(base, new), which means "replace this base version with this new one". Writer B then tries the same from its out-of-date base. Then B retries through the normal API, the library's everyday methods, and the demo appends twice more and travels back in time.
Predict what B's first attempt does, and which metadata file the table ends up at.
Why is the TIMESTAMP AS OF count the same as the first snapshot's?

code.title: CommitDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.batch.l11.demo import org.apache.iceberg.HasTableOperations import org.apache.iceberg.TableMetadata import org.apache.iceberg.exceptions.CommitFailedException import org.apache.iceberg.hadoop.HadoopTables /** * Two writers start from the same version of a table. The first commit wins the swap; the second * is refused, then retried on top of the new version. Then time travel. */ fun main() { val spark = demoSpark() spark.sql("CREATE TABLE lake.pay.ledger ($PAYMENT_COLUMNS) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at))") payments(spark, 0, 1_000).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append() val firstCommitAt = System.currentTimeMillis() Thread.sleep(50) val location = tableDir("pay", "ledger").absolutePath val tables = HadoopTables(spark.sparkContext().hadoopConfiguration()) // two writers load the table: both see the same current version val tableA = tables.load(location) val tableB = tables.load(location) val a = (tableA as HasTableOperations).operations() val b = (tableB as HasTableOperations).operations() val baseA = a.current() val baseB = b.current() println("writer A and writer B both start from ${baseA.metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}") // the low-level commit: "replace base with this new metadata", a compare-and-swap a.commit(baseA, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseA).setProperties(mapOf("settlement.run" to "A")).build()) println("A commits: the table is now at ${a.current().metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}") try { b.commit(baseB, TableMetadata.buildFrom(baseB).setProperties(mapOf("settlement.run" to "B")).build()) } catch (e: CommitFailedException) { println("B commits from the old base: CommitFailedException: ${e.message!!.substringBefore(": /")}") } // the normal API, on B's same stale table object: it reloads the current version, applies // the change to it and swaps; if the swap loses again, it repeats (commit.retry.num-retries) tableB.updateProperties().set("settlement.run", "B").commit() val now = tables.load(location) println("B retries on top of A: the table is at ${(now as HasTableOperations).operations().current().metadataFileLocation().substringAfterLast('/')}, " + "settlement.run = ${now.properties()["settlement.run"]}") // two more appends, then read the past payments(spark, 1_000, 500).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append() payments(spark, 1_500, 500).writeTo("lake.pay.ledger").append() val history = spark.sql("SELECT snapshot_id, parent_id, operation FROM lake.pay.ledger.snapshots ORDER BY committed_at").collectAsList() println("snapshots: " + history.joinToString { "${it.getLong(0)} (${it.getString(2)})" }) println("now: %,d rows".format(spark.table("lake.pay.ledger").count())) println("VERSION AS OF the first snapshot: %,d rows".format( spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM lake.pay.ledger VERSION AS OF ${history.first().getLong(0)}").first().getLong(0))) println("TIMESTAMP AS OF just after the first commit: %,d rows".format( spark.sql("SELECT count(*) FROM lake.pay.ledger TIMESTAMP AS OF CAST($firstCommitAt / 1000.0 AS TIMESTAMP)").first().getLong(0))) spark.stop() }

sections.h: Renaming columns and changing the layout without rewriting a file
sections.html:
Keeping the truth in metadata has two more payoffs. Columns can change without rewriting data, and the way files are grouped becomes part of the table, instead of something every query must remember.

Start with columns. Every column gets its permanent field id when it's created, and Iceberg writes that id into the Parquet files next to the column's name. Readers match a file's columns to the table's by id, not by name. So renaming amount_cents to amount_minor is a metadata change: the id stays the same, old files still match, and no data file is touched. Adding a column gives it a new id that no old file has, so old rows read NULL, the value SQL uses for "nothing here". Dropping a column removes it from the schema, and its data in old files is never read again. Iceberg's documentation lists adding, dropping, renaming and reordering columns, and widening a type (say, from a 32-bit to a 64-bit number), all without rewriting files.

Compare a folder of Parquet files matched by name. Drop amount_cents, add a new amount_cents, and the old values come back from the dead.

Now the grouping. To make a question about one day cheap, tables group their files by day, which is called partitioning. Each day's files sit in their own partition, so a question about one day opens only that day's files. The Hive tables of lesson 4 needed an extra text column, dt, holding the day. A query that filtered on created_at instead of dt read every partition, because Hive didn't know the two were related.

Iceberg partitions by a transform of a real column: PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at)), or hours(...), months(...), truncate(...) and bucket(16, merchant_id). The last one spreads the shops over 16 groups by a hash of their id, a number worked out from the id that scatters ids evenly. There's no extra column. Writers work out the partition value, the manifests record it, and a query that filters on created_at gets the matching days worked out for it. That's hidden partitioning. In the Try it, a one-day filter on created_at plans 1 of the 3 data files.

The grouping itself can change. When a table outgrows its layout, ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(4, merchant_id) starts a new partition spec. New files follow it, and old files keep the spec they were written with. The planner, the part of the engine that decides which files to read, skips each group of files by its own spec. Nothing is rewritten.

All of this is format version 2, which Iceberg 1.12 still creates by default. Format version 3 is adopted in the spec, and Iceberg 1.12 with Spark 4.1 can create and write v3 tables. It adds deletion vectors for removing single rows (the next lesson) and the VARIANT type for JSON from Spark 4 for JVM engineers. It also adds geometry and geography types for points and shapes on a map, default values for columns, times to the nanosecond, and row lineage, a stable _row_id for every row. Ask for it with TBLPROPERTIES ('format-version' = '3'), as the Try it does, once you've checked that every engine that reads the table supports v3.

The table can now grow, travel back in time and change shape. Its weak spot is the single row: correcting one payment means changing a file that must never change.

opening:
Picture a café changing its menu. The owner swaps the price cards on the wall one at a time. A customer who reads the wall halfway through sees new prices for coffee and old ones for cake, a menu that never existed. A careful owner fills a new board in the back room and hangs it in one move.

A table kept as a folder of files works like the first owner. A program adding 200 files drops them in one by one, so a report reading the folder halfway counts part of the job. Each file arrives whole, so the write feels safe, and nothing fails. The trouble is in the gaps between files.

In Warehouses and dimensional models, the warehouse kept each table's file list for us. Here, we'll keep it ourselves with Apache Iceberg, free rules and code for tables made of plain files, so every change appears in one move. We'll also read old versions, and rename a column without touching a file. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a café wall where new and old prices hung side by side. An Iceberg table fills its new board in the back room. It writes every new file first, then moves one pointer, so a reader sees the old table or the new one, never a mix.

Run MetadataTreeDemo again, and open the newest .metadata.json file in labs/bigdata/build/l09/warehouse/pay/payments/metadata with a text editor. Find current-snapshot-id and the list of snapshots. That one number is the whole difference between the table before the last append and the table now.

Next, we'll correct single payments in a table whose files can never change. The question: how do you change one row of a file you can't edit?

drill.prompt: From memory, write the Spark SQL to: create a payments table whose files are grouped by the day of created_at, with hidden partitioning; list its snapshots; read it as of a snapshot id; rename amount_cents to amount_minor; and start grouping new data by merchant_id into 16 buckets. Then say which of the five rewrites a data file.

answer.html: CREATE TABLE lake.pay.payments (payment_id BIGINT, merchant_id INT, amount_cents BIGINT, created_at TIMESTAMP) USING iceberg PARTITIONED BY (days(created_at)); SELECT snapshot_id, parent_id, operation FROM lake.pay.payments.snapshots; SELECT * FROM lake.pay.payments VERSION AS OF 4764547682752508805; ALTER TABLE lake.pay.payments RENAME COLUMN amount_cents TO amount_minor; ALTER TABLE lake.pay.payments ADD PARTITION FIELD bucket(16, merchant_id); -- none of them rewrites a data file: the last two only write a new metadata file, -- and old files keep the partition spec they were written with

recap: A table format keeps the list of a table's files in metadata files next to the data, so readers never list folders, and a write becomes visible in one step.

Iceberg's metadata is a tree of files that are never edited: a pointer, a metadata file (columns, partition specs, snapshots), one manifest list per snapshot, manifests with statistics for each data file, then the Parquet files.

A commit writes new files, then swaps the table's pointer from the old metadata file to the new one. If someone else swapped first, the writer applies its change again and retries: optimistic concurrency.
Every snapshot still lists its files, so VERSION AS OF and TIMESTAMP AS OF read the past, until the snapshot is expired.

Columns are tracked by id, so rename, add and drop only change metadata. Partitions are transforms of real columns (days(created_at)), so queries filter on the column, and the layout can change without rewriting old files.
The limit: files are never edited, so changing one row is still an open problem, and every commit leaves more files and snapshots behind. The next lesson deals with both.

explain.prompt: Explain to someone who knows Hive tables why an Iceberg write is all-or-nothing for readers, using the files the commit writes and the order it writes them in.
explain.answer: A Hive table is its folder: whatever files are in dt=2026-11-03/ right now are the table, so a reader that looks halfway through a write sees half the write. An Iceberg table is whatever its current snapshot lists, and readers find files only through that list. A commit writes in a fixed order. First come the new Parquet data files, which no snapshot names yet, so nobody can see them. Then a manifest that lists those files with their partition values and statistics. Then a new manifest list that names the old manifests plus the new one. Then a new metadata file that adds the snapshot and makes it current. Up to here, every reader still opens the old metadata file and sees the old table. The last step is one swap of the table's pointer from the old metadata file to the new one, which only succeeds if the pointer hasn't moved. In a Hadoop catalog that's a rename that fails if the target exists; in a catalog with a database behind it, it's a conditional update. A reader that starts before the swap sees the old snapshot, one that starts after sees the new one, and none can see a mix. If the job dies before the swap, the files it wrote are orphans that no snapshot lists. They get cleaned up later, and the table never changed.

deeper.html:
The catalog in this lesson is for learning. The Hadoop catalog relies on the file system's rename failing when the target exists, and Iceberg's documentation says it needs a file system with an atomic rename, which object stores like S3 don't offer. Real tables use a catalog that keeps the pointer in a database and does the compare-and-swap there: the Hive Metastore (the catalog service from Hive's era), a JDBC catalog (any database that Java can talk to), AWS Glue (Amazon's catalog service), or a REST catalog server such as Apache Polaris, a free catalog server. The next lesson opens up catalogs and the REST protocol.

Old snapshots cost storage. Every file that any kept snapshot lists stays on disk. CALL system.expire_snapshots(...) removes old snapshots from the metadata and deletes the files only they used, and the time travel window ends there. Small appends also pile up small files and small manifests; rewrite_data_files and rewrite_manifests repack them in a new commit. To bring existing Parquet files into a table without copying them, CALL system.add_files(...) registers them in a commit, and remove_orphan_files deletes files that no snapshot ever listed. The next lesson covers all of these, along with deleting and updating single rows.

Format versions. v1 described tables that only grow; v2 added row-level deletes with delete files; v3, now adopted, adds binary deletion vectors, the VARIANT type (the same one Spark 4 has), geometry and geography types, default column values, row lineage (_row_id, _last_updated_sequence_number) and nanosecond timestamps. Iceberg 1.12 still creates v2 tables unless you set 'format-version' = '3', as the EvolutionDemo does. Version 4 is in development. Its draft replaces the manifest list with a root manifest in a tree that adapts to the table, so a small commit writes fewer metadata files.
